name: Colin Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Colin. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work on the Larchmoor Estate, which is about 900 ewes and a lot of winter wheat and oilseed rape. The owner lives somewhere else, and a farm manager called Ruth runs it with five of us. I'm the junior, so my day is checking sheep on the quad at seven, moving them, footbathing, then whatever needs doing, like carting straw or clearing ditches. I'm still learning to read a sick ewe before she's flat on her side. Ruth can spot one from the gate; I mostly spot them too late.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you end up in farming?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Before this I drove a forklift for fifteen years at a supermarket distribution centre off the motorway. They put in automatic picking, these yellow shuttles running up and down the racks, and they kept half the drivers. I took the money and came out here, because I wanted a job I could see the end of. My partner Asha is a community nurse, and we've got Jakub, who's fourteen, and Leila, who's eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm glad, but I'd also say it still cost my old mates their jobs at the warehouse, hype or not. People forget that the small stuff adds up. I might post that on the local page, and somebody would argue with me under it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it means I keep doing this and get better at it. I'm two years in, and at this rate in five years I might be decent. That's all I want, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic. Keep doing Ruth's lambing course in February, put a bit aside each month like we do now, maybe forty. I'd still use the chatbot now and then to look up a ewe problem before I ring the vet, because it's handy for that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty much how I feel now, which is tired but alright.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use a chatbot now and then. Give me an example from the farm.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last week I had a ewe with a prolapse, and I typed it in to check what I was looking at before I rang Ruth. It was right enough, but Ruth was quicker. The machine told me what it was; Ruth told me what to do with my hands. That's the bit that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still bother you about the job, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pay, and the fact the owner takes the money out and doesn't put much back in. That doesn't change with or without AI. I'd still want a proper wage agreement for farm workers.

S0.say: He'd say he's glad, but point out that even small bits of automation cost his old warehouse mates their jobs. He might post that on the local page and get into an argument.
S0.think: He gets to keep doing the job and getting better at it. Two years in, he hopes to be decent in five.
S0.do: Carries on as now, doing the lambing course in February and saving about forty a month. Keeps using a chatbot now and then to check sheep problems before ringing the vet.
S0.feel: Calm, tired but alright, much like now.
S0.quote: The machine told me what it was; Ruth told me what to do with my hands. That's the bit that matters.
S0.fieldNote: Colin's past as a warehouse forklift driver who lost out to automatic picking makes him alert to small, quiet automation even in the mildest picture. He's a practical, occasional AI user and sees it as a helper, not a replacement for skilled hands. His grievance is with the absentee owner and pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks, that's helpful. The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I've seen this film before at the warehouse, and the people who did well were the ones who got a seat at the table early. I'd tell the lads at Larchmoor to join the union now, not when it's too late. And I'd say the government should tax the machines to pay for training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the estate would buy a robot shepherd thing, a drone or a dog-bot, as soon as it's proven, because the owner loves anything that cuts wages. But there's still lambing, still hands in a ewe at two in the morning. I'd probably keep a job, just a different one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Ruth if I can be the one who learns the new kit when it comes, since I picked up the warehouse scanners quicker than most. I'd use the chatbot more, properly, maybe an evening a week, to learn how these farm systems work. And we'd move the savings up from about two months towards four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. It's familiar, which makes it less scary and more tiring, if that makes sense.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Larchmoor would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably Gary, who's been on the estate thirty years and hates his phone. He's the best stockman there, but if it all goes on a screen, he's done. At the warehouse I watched the best drivers go first, because they were too proud to touch the tablet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Gary if you ended up running the new kit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him I'm not stealing his job, I'm trying to keep mine. And I'd say we should go to Ruth together and make her put training in writing for both of us.

S1.say: He'd say he's seen this before at the warehouse and the people who did well got a seat at the table early. He'd urge workmates to join the union and want machines taxed to pay for training.
S1.think: He expects the estate to buy robot shepherding kit once proven, but believes lambing will still need hands. He'd likely keep a job, just a changed one.
S1.do: Asks the farm manager to make him the one who learns the new kit. Spends an evening a week learning farm systems with the chatbot and pushes savings from about two months towards four.
S1.feel: Uneasy, and tired because it feels so familiar.
S1.quote: At the warehouse I watched the best drivers go first, because they were too proud to touch the tablet.
S1.fieldNote: His warehouse experience gives him a playbook: get close to the new kit early and organise. He worries most about Gary, an older stockman who avoids screens, and wants to go to the manager together rather than compete. A thoughtful mix of self-interest and solidarity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now to the faster pictures. The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we needed rules years ago, and now it's too late to write them. I'd be marching with the union and I'd be saying the government has to step in with income for everyone, right now. I wouldn't be polite about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished at Larchmoor fast. If it can lamb a ewe and drive the drill and spot a sick one from the gate better than Ruth, there's no junior left. And Asha's job, I don't know. People might still want a nurse at the door, but if the robots can do the dressing changes, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the gym, the streaming, the second car, and get the savings sitting where we can see them. I'd go to the council and the job centre in the first month, not wait for the letter. I'd join every union action going, and I'd lean on Asha's mum, who's offered before to help with the kids if we're both out looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the warehouse, only with nowhere to run to this time. Sick in the stomach, mostly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your kids?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jakub's fourteen, he notices everything. I left the warehouse telling him farming was the job they couldn't take off you. I'd have to sit him down and say I got that wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've been through one round of this. Does the speed matter more than the change itself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the difference. With the warehouse they gave us eighteen months' notice and some redundancy money. Two years for everything, everywhere, nobody's offering anything, because nobody's ready.

S2.say: He'd say this is why rules were needed years ago and now it's too late. He'd march with the union and demand government income support for everyone right away.
S2.think: He'd be finished at the estate quickly, and he isn't sure even his partner's nursing job is safe. There'd be no junior role left.
S2.do: Cuts the gym, streaming and the second car to protect savings. Goes to the council and job centre in the first month, joins union actions, and leans on his partner's mother for childcare while they both look for work.
S2.feel: Sick in the stomach, like the warehouse closure but with nowhere to run.
S2.quote: I left the warehouse telling him farming was the job they couldn't take off you. I'd have to sit him down and say I got that wrong.
S2.fieldNote: The most painful part for Colin is that he told his son farming was safe. Two years removes the cushion he had last time, when the warehouse gave eighteen months' notice. He moves fast to cut costs and seek help, which fits his steady but practical nature.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to do this properly if the government gets on with it. I'd be on at the union and at our local representative about retraining money and a shorter working week. I'd say: share the work out, don't throw people away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I think I could find a spot somewhere for a while, maybe minding the machines, but not for long. I'd be forty-eight, and I've already restarted once. The difference is I'd see it coming and could pick the next thing myself instead of having it picked for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd look hard at what's coming and pick a course, probably something on the electrical side, like fixing the robots and chargers, since that's what they'll need for a bit. I'd do it part-time, evenings, the college in town does a level 2 in electrical work. We'd keep saving, aiming for five months, and I'd write to our representative every quarter, I'm not joking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious but alright. It's like knowing lambing's coming: hard, but you can get the shed ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd retrain. Isn't that just a job the AI will also take later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the honest bit. I'd be retraining to fix the robots that took my job, knowing they'll learn to fix themselves too. Buys me a few years, maybe. A few years is worth having with Leila at eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you keep writing to your local representative if nothing came of it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going on our representative. If enough of us write, they have to answer. I know that sounds naïve, but the warehouse redundancy deal only happened because the union pushed for it.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough to do this properly if the government acts. He'd press the union and his local representative for retraining money and a shorter working week so work is shared out.
S3.think: He might find a spot minding machines for a while, but not for long. At 48 he'd at least get to choose the next thing himself.
S3.do: Starts a part-time level 2 electrical course at the town college within the first year, aiming to repair robots and chargers. Builds savings towards five months and writes to his local representative every quarter.
S3.feel: Anxious but alright, like knowing lambing is coming and getting the shed ready.
S3.quote: I'd be retraining to fix the robots that took my job, knowing they'll learn to fix themselves too. Buys me a few years, maybe.
S3.fieldNote: Colin is clear-eyed that retraining to fix robots only buys time, but he values a few years with a young daughter at home. Five years gives him choice, which he didn't have at the warehouse. His faith in political pressure comes from a redundancy deal the union won.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so let's not waste it. I'd want free retraining for anyone over forty, and I'd be loud about it. At work I'd say to the others, start now, don't wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years I can work with. I'd be fifty-three, Jakub grown, Leila nearly done with school, the mortgage down to the last chunk. I could try a couple of things and see what sticks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the electrical course and then something on top, maybe the robot maintenance side or care work, like Asha. I'd talk to Jakub about not doing a trade that a robot will do by the time he's qualified, and maybe help him look at something with people. I'd plan to leave Larchmoor around year five, on my terms, while there's still a job to go to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a fair way. It's a big change but not a mugging.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned care work. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Asha keeps saying I'd be good with people, which is funny coming from a man who talks to sheep all day. I can calm a grumpy ewe; maybe I can calm a grumpy old man in a care home. It's not that different.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Jakub to do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jakub's into engines. I'd tell him by all means learn them, but learn the people bit too, the talking to customers, the explaining. That's what I've noticed lasts longest, every time.

S4.say: He'd call ten years a gift that shouldn't be wasted and push for free retraining for anyone over forty. He'd tell workmates to start now.
S4.think: He can work with ten years: by 53 his children will be mostly grown and the mortgage nearly paid. There's time to try a couple of things.
S4.do: Takes the electrical course and then robot maintenance or care work, and plans to leave the estate around year five on his own terms. Talks to his son about choosing work that involves people.
S4.feel: Uneasy, but he feels it's fair: a big change, not a mugging.
S4.quote: I can calm a grumpy ewe; maybe I can calm a grumpy old man in a care home. It's not that different.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years Colin becomes the planner he couldn't be at the warehouse: a leaving date, a course, advice for his son. His idea that calming a ewe and calming a care home resident are similar was unexpected and warm. He sees people skills as what lasts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I've been through a shutdown with eighteen months' notice and it still flattened me, so two years for the whole world is the one that frightens me. What would help is money coming in while you retrain, a proper income for a couple of years, and a union deal at every farm so the people get a share of what the machines save.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about the owners. Everyone asks us how we'd cope, but nobody asks the man who owns Larchmoor what he owes us when he swaps us out. He's never lambed a ewe in his life, but he'd be the one who decides whether I still have a job.

headlineQuote: He's never lambed a ewe in his life, but he'd be the one who decides whether I still have a job.
portrait: Colin Kowalski is 43, a junior hand on a large sheep and arable estate, two years into farming after a forklift job ended when his warehouse brought in automatic picking. He's progressive, believes in unions and taxing machines, and uses a chatbot now and then for sheep problems. He stays calm or uneasy in the milder pictures and plans to learn the new kit early. AGI in 2 years alarms him because there'd be no notice like he had at the warehouse; with 5 or 10 years he'd retrain on the electrical side or move towards care work, choosing his exit himself. He thinks a lot about his son Jakub and about who owns the machines.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because two years for the whole world is far less warning than the eighteen months he had at the warehouse, which still flattened him.
whatWouldHelp: Income support for a couple of years while people retrain, and a union deal on every farm so workers share what the machines save.
